questions.question:
Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|l|l|} \hline Operator & Precedence & Associativity \\ \hline+ & Highest & Left \\ \hline- & High & Right \\ \hline* & Medium & Right \\ \hline / & Low & Right \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The value of the expression [latex]3+1+5 * 2 / 7+2-4-7-6 / 2 [/latex] as per the above rules is _____
questions.explanation:
Precedence: + (highest) [latex]\gt[/latex] [latex]-[/latex] [latex]\gt[/latex] * [latex]\gt[/latex] / (lowest). The lowest-precedence operator is applied last, so / splits the expression:
[latex](3+1+5*2)\;/\;(7+2-4-7-6)\;/\;2[/latex]

First part: + binds before *, so [latex](3+1+5)*2=9*2=18[/latex].
Second part: + first: [latex]7+2=9[/latex]. Then [latex]-[/latex] is right associative: [latex]9-(4-(7-6))=9-(4-1)=6[/latex].

/ is right associative: [latex]18/(6/2)=18/3=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

questions.question:
Consider a binary tree [latex]T [/latex] in which every node has either zero or two children. Let [latex]n > 0 [/latex] be the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex].
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex] that have exactly two children?
questions.explanation:
In a binary tree where every node has [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children, let [latex]I[/latex] be the number of [latex]2[/latex]-children (internal) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] the number of leaves. A basic counting fact for such trees: [latex]L=I+1[/latex] (each internal node, when added, net-increases the leaf count by exactly one over what it replaced).

Total nodes: [latex]n=I+L=I+(I+1)=2I+1\ \Rightarrow\ I=\dfrac{n-1}2[/latex]

Answer: (n-1)/2

questions.question:
The pseudocode of a function fun() is given below: 

fun(int A[0,...,n-1])
{
    for i=0 to n-2
	for j=0 to n-i-2
	    if (A[j] > A[j+1])
		then swap A[j] and A[j+1]
}
Let [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] be an array storing 30 distinct integers in descending order. The number of swap operations that will be performed, if the function fun() is called with [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] as argument, is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
This is exactly the standard bubble-sort pseudocode. On a fully descending-order array, every single adjacent-pair comparison across the entire double loop finds the pair out of order, so a swap happens on every comparison — there are no comparisons at all that skip the swap.

Total comparisons (and hence swaps) [latex]=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=\binom{n}{2}[/latex] for an [latex]n[/latex]-element array. With [latex]n=30[/latex]: [latex]\binom{30}{2}=\dfrac{30\times29}{2}=435[/latex].

Answer: 435

questions.question:
Consider an unordered list of [latex]N [/latex] distinct integers.
What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
questions.explanation:
We just need to find some element guaranteed not to be the overall largest — not identify the largest itself, and not verify anything about the rest of the list.

Compare any two elements of the list against each other: whichever of the two is smaller is guaranteed to not be the maximum of the whole list (since the larger of this pair beats it, so it can't possibly be the overall largest). This requires only one comparison, and works for any list of [latex]N\ge2[/latex] distinct integers.

Answer: 1

questions.question:
Consider a binary search tree (BST) with [latex]n[/latex] leaf nodes [latex](n>0)[/latex]. Given any node [latex]V[/latex], the key present in the node is denoted as [latex]{Val}(V)[/latex]. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers.

For a node [latex]V[/latex], let [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node [latex]V[/latex] does not have an inorder successor, then [latex]\operatorname{Suc}(V)[/latex] is [latex]N U L L[/latex]. As there are no duplicates, if [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] is not [latex]N U L L[/latex], then [latex]{Val}(V) < {Val}({Suc}(V))[/latex].

Corresponding to every leaf node [latex]L_{i}[/latex] that has a non-NULL [latex]\operatorname{Suc}\left(L_{i}\right)[/latex], a new key [latex]k_{i}[/latex] with the following property is to be inserted into the BST.

[latex] {Val}\left(L_{i}\right) < k_{i} < Val ({Suc}(L_{i}))[/latex]

Let [latex]K[/latex] represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.B: [latex]K[/latex] will have at least one element
options.C: After inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex], the height of the BST can increase at most by one
options.D: Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Since inorder traversal visits keys in strictly increasing order, and [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between two consecutive values in that inorder sequence (a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] and its immediate successor), every such gap [latex](\text{Val}(L_i),\text{Val}(\text{Suc}(L_i)))[/latex] is a distinct, non-overlapping interval — so the chosen [latex]k_i[/latex] values can never coincide. K cannot have duplicates: True.

If the BST has only a single node (which is also its own only leaf, and is simultaneously the overall maximum so it has no inorder successor), then no leaf has a non-NULL successor at all, and [latex]K[/latex] would be empty. So [latex]K[/latex] having at least one element is not always true (fails for the trivial single-node tree).

Since each new key [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] (which has no children) and its successor, the standard BST insertion algorithm places [latex]k_i[/latex] directly as the right child of [latex]L_i[/latex] itself (since [latex]L_i[/latex] has no right subtree to begin with, being a leaf). This adds exactly one extra level below that specific leaf, so the overall tree height increases by at most [latex]1[/latex] (it stays the same unless one of the affected leaves was already at the maximum depth). True.

Since only leaves that have a non-NULL successor get a new key (not every single leaf, and definitely not every internal node), the total node count does not generally double. Not always true.

Answer: K cannot have duplicates; and after inserting all keys of K, the height increases by at most one.

questions.question:
Consider the following pseudo code. What is the total number of multiplications to be performed? 
 D= 2
for i = 1 to n do
   for j = i to n do
      for k = j + 1 to n do
           D = D * 3

options.A: Half of the product of the 3 consecutive integers
options.B: One-third of the product of the 3 consecutive integers.
options.C: One-sixth of the product of the 3 consecutive integers

questions.explanation:
For fixed i and j the innermost loop runs n [latex]-[/latex] j times. Summing over [latex]1\le i\le j\le n[/latex] gives [latex]\binom{n+1}{3}=\frac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{6}[/latex].

That is one-sixth of the product of 3 consecutive integers.

Answer: One-sixth of the product of the 3 consecutive integers

questions.question: The number of possible min-heaps containing each value from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} exactly once is _____.
questions.explanation:
The root must be 1. The 6 remaining numbers split into the left and right subtrees (3 each): [latex]\binom63=20[/latex] ways. In each 3-node subtree the smallest is its root and the other two can be swapped: 2 ways each.

Total = 20 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 80

Answer: 80

Track how [latex]\text{length}\bmod3[/latex] evolves across recursive calls, since only the [latex]\text{length}\%3==1[/latex] branch ever adds [latex]1[/latex] to the final result (the other two branches just recurse without contributing anything):

- If current length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: recurse with length reduced by [latex]1[/latex] (no addition) → new length [latex]\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].
- If current length [latex]\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: add [latex]1[/latex], recurse with length reduced by [latex]1[/latex] → new length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].
- If current length [latex]\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: recurse with length reduced by [latex]2[/latex] (no addition) → new length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].

Once the length's residue enters the cycle [latex]0\to2\to0\to2\to\cdots[/latex], it can never return to residue [latex]1[/latex] again (the only transitions available from [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]2[/latex] both lead back into this same two-value cycle). So the "[latex]+1[/latex]" branch can only ever be triggered once in any call chain — specifically only if the very first (initial) call's length happens to be [latex]\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]. After that single possible addition, the recursion is permanently locked into the non-adding [latex]0/2[/latex] cycle until it terminates at the base case.

So the maximum possible total returned value, over all valid inputs, is just [latex]1[/latex].

Answer: 1
